# Quality control, PCA and batch {#sec-qc} Quality control answers one question: **can we trust the comparison we are about to make?** We look for failed libraries, check that the knockdown worked, and find out which factors drive the largest differences between samples. In particular, we want to know how big the batch effect is compared with the effect of TDP-43 knockdown. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/helpers.R") suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(DESeq2) library(ggplot2) library(pheatmap) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) }) rse <- load_counts_rse() samples <- as.data.frame(colData(rse)[, c("sirna", "batch", "replicate")]) samples$run <- colnames(rse) ``` ::: ## Library size and alignment recount3 ships the STAR alignment statistics for every run. A failed library usually shows up here first: very few reads, a low unique mapping rate, or a very high mitochondrial fraction. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cd <- colData(rse) qc <- data.frame( run = colnames(rse), sirna = cd$sirna, batch = cd$batch, read_pairs = as.numeric(cd$sra.num_spots), unique_pct = as.numeric(cd$`recount_qc.star.uniquely_mapped_reads_%_both`), chrM_pct = as.numeric(cd$`recount_qc.aligned_reads%.chrm`), gene_assigned_pct = as.numeric(cd$`recount_qc.gene_fc.all_%`) ) ggplot(qc, aes(reorder(run, as.integer(sirna)), read_pairs / 1e6, fill = sirna)) + geom_col() + geom_text(aes(label = round(unique_pct)), vjust = -0.3, size = 3) + facet_grid(~ batch, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") + scale_fill_manual(values = SIRNA_COLS) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Read pairs (millions)", fill = "siRNA") + theme_tutorial() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1, size = 8)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Read pairs per run (bars) and the share that STAR mapped uniquely (label). Colour shows the siRNA, facets show the batch.](03-qc_files/figure-html/fig-libsize-1.png){#fig-libsize fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} qc |> group_by(batch) |> summarise(n = n(), median_pairs_M = median(read_pairs) / 1e6, median_unique_pct = median(unique_pct), median_chrM_pct = median(chrM_pct), median_gene_assigned_pct = median(gene_assigned_pct)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|batch | n| median_pairs_M| median_unique_pct| median_chrM_pct| median_gene_assigned_pct| |:-----|--:|--------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|------------------------:| |B1 | 6| 37.78514| 94.75| 5.400| 86.06| |B2 | 12| 16.78675| 95.20| 6.085| 88.28|
::: ::: All libraries map well (more than 94% of read pairs uniquely mapped) and none looks like a failure. The clearest difference is **depth**: B1 runs have roughly twice as many read pairs as B2 runs. Depth is handled by normalisation, but it is our first hint that the two batches were not processed identically. ## Filtering and transformation Raw counts are not suitable for distance-based methods like PCA: the variance of a count grows with its mean, so a few highly expressed genes would dominate. DESeq2's variance stabilising transformation (VST) puts the data on a log2-like scale where the variance is roughly constant [@love2014]. We first drop genes that are too lowly expressed to be informative, with the rule used throughout the book: **at least 10 counts in at least as many samples as the smallest group**. Here we look at all four groups, and the smallest has 3 samples. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds_all <- DESeqDataSet(rse, design = ~ batch + sirna) min_group <- min(table(dds_all$sirna)) keep <- rowSums(counts(dds_all) >= 10) >= min_group dds_all <- dds_all[keep, ] c(min_group_size = min_group, genes_kept = sum(keep), genes_total = length(keep)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> min_group_size genes_kept genes_total #> 3 22837 63856 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # blind = TRUE: the transformation ignores the design, which is what we want # for an unbiased first look at the data. vsd_all <- vst(dds_all, blind = TRUE) ``` ::: ## Did the knockdown work? Before anything else, check the target. If *TARDBP* is not reduced, nothing downstream is interpretable. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds_all <- estimateSizeFactors(dds_all) sym <- rowData(dds_all)$gene_name genes <- c("TARDBP", "STMN2") norm <- counts(dds_all, normalized = TRUE)[match(genes, sym), ] rownames(norm) <- genes as.data.frame(t(norm)) |> mutate(run = colnames(dds_all), sirna = dds_all$sirna, batch = dds_all$batch) |> pivot_longer(all_of(genes), names_to = "gene", values_to = "count") |> ggplot(aes(sirna, count, colour = sirna, shape = batch)) + geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, seed = 1)) + facet_wrap(~ gene, scales = "free_y") + scale_colour_manual(values = SIRNA_COLS, guide = "none") + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Normalised count") + theme_tutorial() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Normalised counts of TARDBP (TDP-43) and of STMN2, a known TDP-43 target, in every sample.](03-qc_files/figure-html/fig-tardbp-1.png){#fig-tardbp fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} kd_eff <- tapply(norm["TARDBP", ], dds_all$sirna, mean) round(kd_eff) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> none fluorescent scramble TDP43 #> 2741 2656 2615 1031 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(100 * (1 - kd_eff["TDP43"] / kd_eff["scramble"])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> TDP43 #> 61 ``` ::: ::: *TARDBP* mRNA is about 61% lower in the knockdown than in scramble, in both batches. A partial knockdown is typical for siRNA. Note that mRNA level is not protein level; the original study measured the protein, but RNA-seq alone cannot. *STMN2*, one of the best known TDP-43 targets, is also lower, which is a first sign that the knockdown had functional consequences in these cells. ## Principal component analysis PCA finds the directions of largest variation among samples. We use the 500 most variable genes after VST, a common default. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_data <- function(mat, ntop = 500) { rv <- apply(mat, 1, var) top <- order(rv, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(min(ntop, length(rv)))] pc <- prcomp(t(mat[top, ])) list(x = as.data.frame(pc$x[, 1:4]), var = round(100 * pc$sdev^2 / sum(pc$sdev^2), 1)) } ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- pca_data(assay(vsd_all)) pdat <- cbind(p$x, as.data.frame(colData(vsd_all)[, c("sirna", "batch")])) ggplot(pdat, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = sirna, shape = batch)) + geom_point(size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = SIRNA_COLS) + labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", p$var[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", p$var[2], "%)"), colour = "siRNA", shape = "Batch") + theme_tutorial() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![PCA of all 18 samples (VST, 500 most variable genes). Colour shows the siRNA, shape shows the batch.](03-qc_files/figure-html/fig-pca-1.png){#fig-pca fig-align='center'} ::: ::: Which factor does each principal component follow? A quick way to put a number on it is the R² of a linear model of each PC on batch or on siRNA group. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} r2 <- function(pc, f) summary(lm(pc ~ f))$r.squared sapply(paste0("PC", 1:4), function(k) c(variance_pct = p$var[as.integer(sub("PC", "", k))], R2_batch = r2(pdat[[k]], pdat$batch), R2_sirna = r2(pdat[[k]], pdat$sirna))) |> round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4 #> variance_pct 63.40 11.80 7.20 6.30 #> R2_batch 0.88 0.02 0.00 0.01 #> R2_sirna 0.05 0.48 0.31 0.74 ``` ::: ::: Read the plot and the table together: - **PC1 separates the two batches.** It carries 63% of the variance and batch explains almost all of it (R² close to 0.9). The batch effect is the largest single source of variation in this data set. - **The siRNA groups are spread over PC2 to PC4**, and within each batch the knockdown samples tend to sit apart from the controls, but no single component cleanly separates knockdown from control while batch dominates. This is exactly why the design table in @sec-design mattered: because the groups are balanced across batches, the batch effect can be modelled. ## Sample correlation heatmap A correlation heatmap shows the same structure from another angle: every sample against every other. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cors <- cor(assay(vsd_all), method = "pearson") ann <- as.data.frame(colData(vsd_all)[, c("sirna", "batch")]) pheatmap(cors, annotation_col = ann, annotation_row = ann, annotation_colors = list(sirna = SIRNA_COLS, batch = c(B1 = "grey30", B2 = "grey80")), show_colnames = FALSE, fontsize_row = 7, color = colorRampPalette(c("white", "#1f5f8b"))(50)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Pearson correlation between samples (VST values of all filtered genes), clustered hierarchically.](03-qc_files/figure-html/fig-corr-1.png){#fig-corr fig-align='center'} ::: ::: All correlations are very high (above 0.97), which is normal for samples of one cell type; what matters is the clustering. The samples split first by batch. Within B2, the four knockdown samples form their own branch, the fluorescent-siRNA pair clusters together, and the untransfected pair clusters with two of the scramble samples. ## Looking past the batch effect To see the knockdown effect more clearly, we can remove the batch effect **for visualisation only** with `limma::removeBatchEffect()` [@ritchie2015]. We give it the design for the biology we want to keep, so that it does not remove group differences that happen to correlate with batch. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mat <- limma::removeBatchEffect(assay(vsd_all), batch = vsd_all$batch, design = model.matrix(~ sirna, colData(vsd_all))) p2 <- pca_data(mat) pdat2 <- cbind(p2$x, as.data.frame(colData(vsd_all)[, c("sirna", "batch")])) ggplot(pdat2, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = sirna, shape = batch)) + geom_point(size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = SIRNA_COLS) + labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", p2$var[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", p2$var[2], "%)"), colour = "siRNA", shape = "Batch") + theme_tutorial() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![PCA after removing the batch effect from the VST values (for display only).](03-qc_files/figure-html/fig-pca-corrected-1.png){#fig-pca-corrected fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} with(pdat2, round(c(highest_PC2_knockdown = max(PC2[sirna == "TDP43"]), lowest_PC2_scramble_or_fluorescent = min(PC2[sirna %in% c("scramble", "fluorescent")])), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> highest_PC2_knockdown lowest_PC2_scramble_or_fluorescent #> -0.9 0.0 ``` ::: ::: After batch correction, the knockdown samples separate from the scramble and fluorescent controls, along PC1 and PC2 together: every knockdown sample has a lower PC2 value than every scramble and fluorescent sample. Two further details are worth noticing: - The knockdown samples are spread along PC1: three of them move much further from the controls than the other three, even though their *TARDBP* levels look similar. Response heterogeneity between cultures is normal and is exactly what replicates are for. - The two untransfected (none) samples from B2 sit apart from all transfected samples at the bottom of the plot. Transfection itself changes the transcriptome a little, which confirms that scramble siRNA, not "no siRNA", is the right control for the knockdown. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Never run DE on batch-corrected values `removeBatchEffect()` returns adjusted log-scale values. Feeding them to a DE test would treat the correction as if it were data and give over-confident p-values. For DE we put `batch` in the model instead (`~ batch + condition`, @sec-de), so the uncertainty of the batch estimate is accounted for. ::: ## Other covariates The metadata contain no per-sample RIN or differentiation efficiency. The protocol only says that all libraries had RIN above 7.5. Sex is easy to check from the data themselves, using *XIST* (expressed from the inactive X in female cells) and genes on the Y chromosome: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sex_genes <- c("XIST", "RPS4Y1", "DDX3Y", "KDM5D") raw <- counts(DESeqDataSet(rse, design = ~ 1)) lib_m <- colSums(raw) / 1e6 cpm_sex <- sapply(sex_genes, function(g) raw[which(rowData(rse)$gene_name == g)[1], ] / lib_m) round(apply(cpm_sex, 2, range), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> XIST RPS4Y1 DDX3Y KDM5D #> [1,] 0.0 100.6 43 28.6 #> [2,] 0.1 124.4 73 43.1 ``` ::: ::: *XIST* is essentially absent and the Y-linked genes are expressed in every sample, so all 18 samples come from a male cell line, and sex does not need a covariate. A sample that disagreed would point to a sample swap. If your own data have covariates, check them the same way as batch: colour the PCA by each one and compute the R² with the leading PCs. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} saveRDS(dds_all, cache_path("dds_all_18_samples.rds")) ``` ::: ## Decisions for the next chapters | Question | Answer from QC | Consequence | |---|---|---| | Failed libraries? | None | Keep all samples | | Knockdown worked? | *TARDBP* reduced in every knockdown sample | Proceed | | Largest source of variation | Batch (PC1) | Model it: `~ batch + condition` | | Controls behave alike? | Scramble and fluorescent alike; untransfected slightly apart | Scramble is the right control | | Sex | All samples male (Y genes on, *XIST* off) | No covariate needed | | Confounding? | No, balanced design | Batch effect is estimable | ::: {.callout-tip} ## Check your understanding 1. Why do we run PCA on VST values rather than on raw or normalised counts? 2. PC1 separates the batches. Does that mean the data are unusable? 3. Why is `blind = TRUE` appropriate for QC, and when would you use `blind = FALSE`? 4. A labmate suggests running DESeq2 on the output of `removeBatchEffect()`. What do you answer? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Answers 1. Counts have variance that grows with the mean, so distances would be dominated by a few highly expressed genes. VST makes the variance roughly independent of the mean. 2. No. Batch effects are common. They are a problem when they are confounded with the biology or ignored. Here the design is balanced and we model the batch. 3. `blind = TRUE` ignores the design, so the QC view is not shaped by what we expect to see. `blind = FALSE` uses the design to estimate the dispersion trend, which is preferable for downstream plots such as heatmaps when large group differences exist. 4. Do not. Corrected values are not counts, and the test would ignore the uncertainty of the correction. Include batch in the design formula. ::: :::
